title: Japan's AMRAAM assembly line, Britain's doubled submarine rate, and Turkey co-founding a $100bn defence bank
subhead: Tokyo won final assembly of the AIM-120 after two years of export-control bargaining, the Submarine Delivery Agency put a doubling target on UK SSN-AUKUS output, and nine governments including Greece and Turkey will sign the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank into existence in Luxembourg on November 30.

sections.heading: Japan gets final assembly of AMRAAM — a commitment without a site or an output figure
sections.body:
Japan will host final assembly and checkout of the U.S. AIM-120 AMRAAM, Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi announced on October 28 after meeting U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the sidelines of a Southeast Asian defence ministers' meeting in Cebu, Philippines. Koizumi called it a 'groundbreaking agreement' that secures equipment for both countries and strengthens Japan's defence industrial base, describing the radar-guided missile as 'essential for the F-35'. A Pentagon readout of the meeting did not mention the AMRAAM deal at all, per an analysis by SOFX, and Koizumi named no site, no industrial partner, no construction timeline and no output figure. Janes separately confirmed the two sides agreed to establish the final assembly and checkout facility.

The groundwork is real, if slow. The two governments agreed in July 2024 to explore joint AMRAAM and PAC-3 production, and Japan's Acquisition, Technology and Logistics Agency ran a feasibility study with Mitsubishi Electric and Raytheon. In April 2026 the partners identified circuit card assembly — the missile's electronic boards — as Japan's initial production share, and Mitsubishi Electric said that month it was pursuing the final-assembly role. Approval took more than two years, held up by Japan's postwar limits on exporting lethal equipment and by the missile's classified guidance technology.

The scale of the gap this fills is large. In late September the Pentagon awarded Raytheon a five-year contract worth up to $20.7 billion, with two option years, and a February framework calls for lifting U.S. AMRAAM output to at least 1,900 missiles a year. Japan separately had State Department approval in January 2025 for up to 1,200 AIM-120s at an estimated $3.64 billion.
sections.whyItMatters: This is licensed assembly, not co-development — Japan gets the industrial base and the stockpile proximity, Washington gets a second production node without releasing guidance secrets. The absence of any site, partner or volume figure means the announcement buys political credit now and defers every hard industrial decision.

sections.heading: SM-3 Block IIA: the more consequential half of the Cebu package
sections.body:
Announced in the same breath, and almost entirely overshadowed: the two governments agreed to share technical information to expand production of the SM-3 Block IIA, the ship-launched interceptor that kills ballistic missiles in space, co-developed by Raytheon and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. The two sides agreed in March 2026 to quadruple output in Japan, and Tokyo covered close to half of a $745 million order this summer. As with the AMRAAM, neither government set output targets, delivery schedules or a start date.

Read together, the two announcements describe a single problem: allied interceptor magazines are being drawn down faster than the U.S. industrial base can replace them, and the fix being applied across the Indo-Pacific is to push production to the ally that will also be the customer.
sections.whyItMatters: SM-3 Block IIA is the higher-end interceptor and the one with a live production constraint. Quadrupling Japanese output matters more for regional magazine depth than an unspecified AMRAAM line — but both remain announcements rather than capacity until dates and volumes exist.

sections.heading: Britain targets double submarine output against a 12-boat SSN-AUKUS requirement
sections.body:
Sir Chris Gardner, chief executive of the UK's Submarine Delivery Agency, said Britain is seeking to double its submarine production rate to meet a requirement for up to 12 SSN-AUKUS attack submarines for the Royal Navy. 'This marks our ambition to enable continuous submarine production in the UK,' Gardner said, though the agency did not specify a deadline for reaching that rate. The figures are set out in the SDA's Annual Report and Accounts 2025/2026, presented to Parliament in October 2026 — which describes the intended expansion but does not report that a doubled rate has been achieved.

A new Submarine Production Alliance will run Dreadnought and SSN-AUKUS as a single portfolio, uniting the government's Submarine Delivery Group with BAE Systems, Rolls-Royce Submarines and Babcock International. Expansion requires more capacity at Barrow-in-Furness, Rolls-Royce's Raynesway site and the supplier base — while all four Dreadnought ballistic-missile submarines are still under construction. Dreadnought build work passed one million hours in 2025, three times the 2023 level, and all units for the first boat have moved to the Devonshire Dock Hall at Barrow for final outfitting.

The report flags supplier fragility directly: the agency said it is working with industry to identify vulnerabilities, and in the motors category it has introduced additional suppliers to break single-source reliance. A Preliminary Design Review for SSN-AUKUS in 2026 is named as the key step toward production. The UK-Australia arrangement is governed by a treaty signed in July 2025 covering a 50-year partnership.
sections.whyItMatters: Doubling submarine output is the hardest industrial ask in British defence — one yard, one reactor supplier, a nuclear deterrent programme running in parallel, and a supply chain already being patched on motors. The Alliance is a coordination answer to a capacity problem, and the report's own language concedes the rate has not yet moved.

sections.heading: Nine states will sign a defence bank into existence on November 30 — with $100bn in mind and no AAA rating yet
sections.body:
Albania, Belgium, Canada, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania, Turkey and Ukraine have confirmed their intention to establish the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), with the founding agreement scheduled to be signed in Luxembourg on November 30, according to Greek outlet To Vima. The institution is expected to begin operations in 2027. It follows the Ankara Declaration of July 7, with founding articles negotiated in Montreal in April.

The bank is aimed at widening access to capital, cutting financing costs and expanding defence-industrial capacity, and is pitched as complementing — not duplicating — national and multilateral lenders. It is expected to raise up to €100 billion for affordable project finance and guarantees for lenders backing smaller companies. Two caveats are explicit: the participants want a AAA credit rating but have not obtained one, and Britain has decided not to join, citing unresolved differences over governance, joint procurement and lending arrangements — although London and Ottawa intend to build a framework linking their separate defence-financing initiatives.

The membership list is the story. Greece and Turkey sit in the same founding bloc while both run parallel modernization programmes and remain at odds in the Aegean and eastern Mediterranean. Greece plans roughly €28 billion of defence spending through 2036, covering 20 F-35s, further F-16 upgrades, 35 Black Hawks, the Israeli-equipped Achilles Shield air-and-missile defence system and four French Belharra-class frigates. Turkey is lobbying to buy 20 Eurofighter Typhoons from the UK and pursuing additional aircraft from Qatar and Oman, alongside a domestic fighter programme.
sections.whyItMatters: A lender designed to finance defence capacity across a 2027 horizon is a structural change to how European procurement gets paid for — but the missing AAA rating and Britain's abstention mean the first real test will be whether it can price a loan cheaply enough to beat national budgets.

sections.heading: China lands the GJ-21 stealth drone on the Sichuan — the first large stealth UAV recovered by an amphibious assault ship
sections.body:
China's GJ-21 reconnaissance-strike stealth drone completed its first takeoff and landing aboard the Sichuan, the first Type 076 amphibious assault ship, Xinhua reported. Beijing-based analyst Zhang Xuefeng, speaking to the Global Times, called it the world's first catapult launch and recovery of a large stealth strike and reconnaissance drone from an amphibious assault ship.

Zhang's description of the aircraft: a flying-wing configuration with an S-shaped top-mounted air intake to cut radar returns, giving all-aspect stealth he rates as superior to in-service stealth fighters; a subsonic cruise-efficient wing that yields a combat radius comparable to the J-20 and J-35 despite a far smaller airframe; and reusability, carrying small low-cost glide-guided bombs rather than being expended like a hypersonic missile. He framed its role as a 'door-kicking' vanguard for suppression of enemy air defences, pairing with manned fighters that clear an air corridor while the GJ-21 works over ground targets and air-defence sites.

The Sichuan, hull number 51, is China's first independently designed Type 076. Launched and named on December 27, 2024, it carries an electromagnetic catapult and arresting gear, a fully automated landing guidance system and a new integrated power system, and can operate fixed-wing drones, helicopters and amphibious equipment. It began sea trials in November 2025.

Treat the performance claims with care: the stealth and combat-radius comparisons come from a Chinese analyst commenting to a state-aligned outlet, not from independently verified data. The takeoff and landing themselves are attributable to Xinhua.
sections.whyItMatters: A drone carrier changes the arithmetic of Chinese naval aviation. A Type 076 carrying stealth UAVs gives the PLAN a cheaper way to project fixed-wing strike and SEAD than building more carriers — and an exportable, reusable product that costs a fraction of a crewed naval fighter.

sections.heading: Kim shows off suicide drones and calls AI dominance 'indispensable'
sections.body:
North Korea test-fired attack drones, missiles and a 600mm multiple rocket launcher at a weapons demonstration, state media reported on Friday, October 30, per Channel NewsAsia. The display featured suicide attack drones, multipurpose drones firing air-to-surface missiles, cruise missiles and the 600mm rocket launchers; KCNA said the drones and cruise missiles hit an island target with '100 per cent accuracy'.

Kim Jong Un's framing was explicitly about industrial direction, not just deterrence: seizing 'absolute superiority in the drone technology is an indispensable option in the light of the ever-changing patterns of modern warfare', KCNA quoted him as saying. He added that 'strength precisely means peace'. The event came a day after South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff detected around a dozen short-range ballistic missiles fired from the Wonsan area toward the East Sea, flying about 250 km; Seoul's military and the U.S. said they were still analysing the specifications and could not immediately confirm whether the launches were part of the demonstration. Seoul's National Security Office called the launches a violation of UN Security Council resolutions.

Pyongyang has now tied AI to three separate systems in recent weeks: the drones on display, a new precision-guided torpedo system, and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile, all described as employing AI technology.
sections.whyItMatters: North Korea is describing autonomy and AI as the target capability rather than as an add-on. What it actually fields may lag the rhetoric, but the stated procurement priority — cheap, mass-produced attritable systems — is the same conclusion Western armies reached after Ukraine, and it is being funded on a sanctions-constrained budget.

sections.heading: Hanwha's first U.S. Navy shipbuilding award, and France turning tank gunners into FPV pilots
sections.body:
Two industrial data points that say more about where capacity and doctrine are moving than any single contract announcement.

Hanwha Defense USA received its first U.S. Navy shipbuilding contract: $269 million to build a Medium Landing Ship at Hanwha Philly Shipyard, with options for three more and construction starting in the fourth quarter of 2027. TOTE Services picked Hanwha as the first builder under its Vessel Construction Manager contract, part of a $2.2 billion arrangement supporting a planned fleet of 35 Medium Landing Ships, the first of which is expected in 2030. Hanwha acquired the Philadelphia yard in 2024 and is moving to take a controlling stake in it, announced this week. The yard has already delivered four National Security Multi-Mission Vessels under the same management model.

In France, the Army is converting gunner crews into drone operators. The 1er RIMa turned one of its three light cavalry squadrons into an experimental all-drone unit — the 1er Escadron de Drones de Chasse — and the results pushed the service to scale. Army Chief of Staff Gen. Jacques de Montgros told lawmakers on October 14 that the aim is around 15 drone-combat units by summer 2027; Gen. Bruno Baratz, head of Future Combat Command, said six will be operational in 2027, and 6th Armored Brigade commander Gen. Maxime do Tran said his brigade created a third unit from its own resources without waiting. France deployed a drone-combat unit to Romania under Mission Aigle and will send a second to Poland next month, per Defense News.

The exercise data is the argument: at Exercise Hedgehog in Estonia in May 2025, French drone pilots made up roughly 5% of the tactical group's strength but inflicted about 20% of the attrition on the opposing force. In a March 2026 exercise at Mailly-le-Camp, the squadron virtually destroyed an opposing force's armour and tracked vehicles to command posts and troop concentrations.
sections.whyItMatters: Hanwha's award is the clearest sign yet that Washington will buy allied-built hulls at allied speed when U.S. yards are full — a quiet shift in how the Navy sources. France's units are the other half: an army reorganizing its order of battle around the finding that a handful of FPV pilots can produce a fifth of the damage.

bottomLine: Three of today's developments are the same move made in three different currencies: Japan gets licensed AMRAAM and SM-3 assembly, Britain targets double submarine output through a single production alliance, and nine governments will sign a €100bn-capacity defence bank into existence in Luxembourg on November 30. All three are attempts to buy industrial capacity rather than equipment, and all three have the same weakness — no site, no date, no rating, or no achieved rate. In parallel, China has now demonstrated recoverable stealth strike drones from a Type 076 amphibious ship, North Korea has declared AI and drone dominance a procurement priority, and France is disbanding gunner crews to build fifteen drone squadrons by mid-2027. The procurement question of the year is no longer which system to buy; it is who can actually build it, how fast, and who pays for the factory.
sources: SOFX (citing Japan Ministry of Defense, U.S. Department of War readout, Mitsubishi Electric, Breaking Defense, Air & Space Forces Magazine), Janes, Defence Industry Europe (Submarine Delivery Agency Annual Report 2025/2026; Hanwha/TOTE Services), To Vima (Greece/Turkey DSRB), Xinhua via Global Times (GJ-21/Sichuan), Channel NewsAsia (KCNA, South Korea JCS), Defense News (French Army drone squadrons)
